options.why: The Vote of Confidence is not a temperature check that the facilitator records and moves past. Members who rate one or two explain their concerns, and the entire Agile Project Core Team then performs the required adjustments to address them; the ceremony ends only when there are no more ones or twos (p.44). The adjustment is the point of the vote. An eight-hour spike bought with capacity the team already holds is exactly what the step is for, and it turns a corridor remark into a plan.
options.whyPlain: The Vote of Confidence is not a mood check that the facilitator notes and passes over. People who vote one or two explain their concerns, and then the whole team makes the changes needed to answer them. The ceremony ends only when there are no ones or twos left (page 44). The change is the purpose of the vote. Spending eight hours the team already has on a spike is exactly what this step is for, and it turns a corridor remark into a plan.
ref: should explain their concerns and doubts

options.t: Record the concern in the Risk Log and close the planning. Four people out of five are comfortable and the timebox has ten minutes left.

options.why: Logging a concern is not adjusting for it. The guide's fifth step is explicit that after the ones and twos have spoken, the entire A-PCT performs the required adjustments to address those concerns, and the vote closes only when none remain (p.44). Carrying an unaddressed two into an iteration converts a known problem into a mid-iteration surprise, and the daily stand-up will surface it again on day four at a worse cost.
options.whyPlain: Writing a concern down is not the same as acting on it. The guide's fifth step says that after the ones and twos have spoken, the whole team makes the changes needed to answer them, and the vote closes only when no ones or twos are left (page 44). Carrying an unanswered vote of two into the iteration turns a known problem into a surprise later. The daily stand-up will raise it again on day four, when it costs more.
ref: Once all the concerns are discussed and there are no more "1's" or "2's", the Vote of Confidence ends

options.why: The split is deliberate. The Product Owner proposes and is Accountable for the Iteration Goal; the Agile Team Members are Responsible for the Iteration Planning itself, and decide how the work will be done (p.45 RAM, p.64). PM²-Agile's self-organising team holds the plan, and the adjustment after a vote of confidence belongs to the whole A-PCT, not to the role that set the goal.
options.whyPlain: The split is deliberate. The Product Owner proposes the Iteration Goal and is Accountable for it. The Agile Team Members are Responsible for the planning itself and decide how the work is done (page 45 and page 64). In PM²-Agile the team organises itself and owns the plan, so the change after a vote of confidence belongs to the whole team, not to the person who set the goal.
ref: Iteration Planning I I S S/A S R

options.why: The fourth stand-up question and the confidence vote are both framed against the iteration goal, not against individual comfort: the vote asks how confident members are in the proposed plan as a whole (pp.44, 46). Reassigning the dissenter removes the voice and keeps the risk. The guide's response to a low vote is an adjustment to the plan agreed by the whole team, then another vote.
options.whyPlain: Both the fourth stand-up question and the confidence vote are about the iteration goal, not about personal comfort. The vote asks how confident each person is in the whole proposed plan (pages 44 and 46). Moving the person who disagrees removes the warning and keeps the risk. The guide answers a low vote with a change to the plan agreed by the whole team, followed by another vote.
ref: How confident am I that we will accomplish the iteration goal?

note: Guide check: section 5.1, pp.41-45. Iteration Planning is the first activity of the iteration and is sized at two hours for each iteration week — four hours for a two-week iteration. Its mandatory input is a prioritised Work Items List with acceptance criteria already defined; prioritising the list is Release Planning's job, not this ceremony's. The five steps are: determine the team's capacity in hours, allowing for holidays and an allowance for unplanned events; agree the Iteration Goal, which the Product Owner defines from the prioritised list; define the work to be done, decomposing items into tasks of no more than twelve hours, each taken by a named member, with the stop rule when nobody can take a task; the Commitment Agreement, in one of three scenarios; and the Vote of Confidence, one to five on a hand count, ending only when no one is on one or two. RASCI p.45: BM I, PM I, TeCo S, PrOw S/A, ArOw S, ATeM R. Approver: the Product Owner is accountable for the goal; the team is responsible for the plan. Pages 41-45.
notePlain: Rule: Iteration Planning is the first thing the team does in an iteration, and it lasts about two hours for each week of the iteration. So a two-week iteration gets four hours (page 42). It needs a Work Items List that is already in priority order, with acceptance criteria written. Putting the list in order is done in Release Planning, not here. There are five steps. First, each person works out their capacity in hours, after holidays and an allowance for unplanned work (pages 43 and 45). Second, the Product Owner sets the Iteration Goal from the prioritised list. Third, the team breaks items into tasks of twelve hours or less, and each task is taken by one person; if nobody can take a task, the team stops adding work (pages 43 and 44). Fourth, the Commitment Agreement, where the goal may be made smaller. Fifth, the Vote of Confidence, a hand count from one to five, which ends only when nobody votes one or two. Who is who: the team members are Responsible, the Product Owner is Accountable for the goal, the Team Coordinator only Supports, and the Project Manager is only Informed. Pages 41 to 45.

options.why: The Daily Stand-up is neither a status update meeting nor a problem-solving meeting, and the Project Manager is Informed of its outcomes rather than a participant in a status round (pp.45, 47). Status has its own artefact: the Development Status Report, produced by the Team Coordinator, accountable to the Project Manager, carrying cost, schedule, scope, risks and both burndown charts, and folded into the Project Status Report (p.83). Coordination between the agile team and other stakeholders is exactly what PM²-Agile adjusts the format and frequency of reporting for.
options.whyPlain: The Daily Stand-up is not a status meeting and not a problem-solving meeting, and the Project Manager is only Informed of what came out of it (pages 45 and 47). Status has its own document: the Development Status Report. The Team Coordinator writes it, the Project Manager is Accountable for it, and it carries cost, schedule, scope, risks and both burndown charts (page 83). PM²-Agile adjusts the format and frequency of reporting for exactly this kind of audience.
ref: Daily Stand-up N/A I S I R R/A

options.why: The guide states plainly that the ceremony is neither a status update meeting nor a problem-solving meeting; each member answers four questions, and all four are framed against the iteration goal (pp.45-46). A status round appended to it changes the audience, and with the audience the honesty. The RAM makes the point structurally: the ATeMs are Responsible and Accountable for the Stand-up, the PM is only Informed, and the Business Manager is the single N/A in the ceremony tables.
options.whyPlain: The guide says clearly that this ceremony is not a status meeting and not a problem-solving meeting. Each member answers four questions, and all four are about the iteration goal (pages 45 and 46). Adding a status round changes who the audience is, and that changes how honest people are. The responsibility table makes the same point: the team members are Responsible and Accountable for the Stand-up, the Project Manager is only Informed, and the Business Manager is marked not applicable.

note: Guide check: sections 4.11 to 4.13, pp.37-40, with the Definition of Done at p.88 and the Test Plan at p.81. Development rests on three complementary practices: Continuous Integration, where members integrate at least daily so integration issues are found and fixed while the change is fresh; Evolutionary Design; and Test-Driven Development, in which test cases are created before the code and act as guardrails. Testing is iterative and incremental — test early and test often, in every iteration, with tests run against each build deployed to the mainline. Software Configuration Management identifies every item, controls change, versions it, audits it and reports it, so that a specific version of the solution can be rebuilt and quality is maintained as the configuration evolves. The Definition of Done is the team's own agreed set of conditions for a Work Item to count as complete; it belongs to the Agile Team Members, not to a manager. RASCI p.81: Test Plan BM I, PM A, TeCo S, PrOw S, ArOw S, ATeM R — the only agile artefact row where an Agile Team Member is Responsible and the Team Coordinator merely Supports. Pages 37-40, 81, 88.
notePlain: Rule: development in PM²-Agile uses three practices together. Continuous Integration means everyone merges their work at least once a day, so integration problems are found early and fixed while the change is still fresh (page 37). Evolutionary Design means the design grows and is refactored. Test-Driven Development means the test cases are written before the code, so the code must pass them (page 38). Testing is iterative: test early and test often, in every iteration, with tests run against each build sent to the mainline (pages 39 and 40). Software Configuration Management identifies every item, controls and versions changes, audits them and reports them, so any version can be rebuilt and quality is kept as things change (page 38). The Definition of Done is the team's own list of conditions for a work item to count as complete (page 88). Who is who on the Test Plan: the team members are Responsible, the Project Manager is Accountable, and the Team Coordinator only Supports. Pages 37 to 40, 81 and 88.

note: Guide check: section 5.4, pp.52-56, with the Definition of Done at p.88. The Iteration Review assesses whether the iteration goal was achieved, by demonstrating what was built; it is a closure ceremony on the last day of the iteration, 90 to 120 minutes for a two-week iteration. It has three moments. Align expectations: a ten to fifteen minute presentation by an Agile Team Member covering scope, achieved, not achieved, new and dropped items, and difficulties. Demo: single-point or hands-on, decided in advance, with the test scenarios agreed beforehand; for each item, describe it with its acceptance criteria, demonstrate each scenario naming the criterion it validates, then ask for confirmation that it is Done. Technical and enabler work must be demonstrated too, because it is invisible and the Product Owner must understand its impact. Then wrap-up and Work Items List review. Acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done are different instruments: the first is what the item must do, the second is the team's own quality standard for any item to count as complete. RASCI p.56: BIG C, BM C, PM I, TeCo S, PrOw A/S, ArOw R, ATeM R. Pages 52-56, 88.
notePlain: Rule: the Iteration Review checks whether the iteration goal was reached, by showing what was built. It is a closing meeting on the last day of the iteration, and 90 to 120 minutes is good practice for a two-week iteration (page 53). It has three parts. First, align expectations: a ten to fifteen minute talk by a team member covering the goal and committed items, what was achieved, what was not, new and dropped items, and difficulties (pages 53 and 54). Second, the demonstration. The team decides in advance whether stakeholders watch or use it themselves, and which test scenarios are used. For each item: describe it with its acceptance criteria, demonstrate each scenario and name the criterion it proves, then ask for confirmation that it is Done (page 54). Technical and enabler work must be shown too, because it is invisible and the Product Owner needs to understand it (page 56). Third, the wrap-up. Acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done are different things. The first is what the item must do. The second is the team's own quality standard for any item to count as complete (page 88). Who is who: team members and the Architecture Owner are Responsible, the Product Owner is Accountable, the Business Manager and user representatives are Consulted, and the Project Manager is Informed. Pages 52 to 56 and 88.

note: Guide check: section 5.5, pp.57-60. The Iteration Retrospective happens at the end of every iteration, lasts 60 to 120 minutes depending on team size, iteration size and the level of stress, and follows five steps. Welcome, which the guide calls the most important: each member says in one sentence how the iteration felt, because if silence is allowed here it rules the rest of the meeting; the facilitator states the timebox and the rules, reusing the team's working agreements. Collect Hard Data: events and metrics — burndown, velocity, broken builds, test coverage — with feelings attached to the timeline; the Team Coordinator helps collect, but the Agile Team Members decide which data to use. Understand Data and Generate Ideas: root causes and alternatives. Prioritise and Choose: a few actions the team can commit to, added to the Work Items List so they are treated like any other item, each with a named member rather than the team. Closing: the learnings belong to the members, and everything is recorded in a Retrospective Log that later enriches the Lessons Learned. RASCI p.60: BM I, PM I, TeCo S, PrOw I, ArOw R, ATeM R/A. Pages 57-60.
notePlain: Rule: the Iteration Retrospective happens at the end of every iteration and lasts 60 to 120 minutes, depending on the size of the team, the length of the iteration and how much stress there was (page 57). It has five steps. First, Welcome, which the guide calls the most important: each person says in one sentence how the iteration felt, because if silence is allowed here it will rule the whole meeting. The facilitator states the timebox and the rules, using the team's working agreements (page 58). Second, Collect Hard Data: events and measurements such as burndown, velocity, broken builds and test coverage, with feelings added to the timeline. The Team Coordinator helps collect it, but the team members choose which data to use (pages 58 and 59). Third, understand the data and generate ideas. Fourth, prioritise and choose a few actions the team can commit to, put them in the Work Items List, and give each one a named person, because a task given to the team gets nobody to do it (page 59). Fifth, close: the learnings belong to the team members, and everything is recorded in a Retrospective Log that later feeds the Lessons Learned (pages 59, 60 and 57). Pages 57 to 60.

note: Guide check: section 7.3.1, pp.83-85, with section 4.3, pp.29-30. The Development Status Report documents the status of the Agile Project Core Team towards the development goals and is incorporated at project reporting level, carrying cost, schedule, scope, risks, issues, changes and forecasts; it can follow each iteration and each release. Its key element is the burndown chart at two levels. The iteration burndown chart tracks remaining effort in points or hours, is the primary tool for understanding the current iteration and should be updated frequently, preferably daily, so the team can react — by reducing scope, reducing the ambition of a work item, or finding a better approach. The release burndown chart tracks functionality rather than effort, and shows whether the team is delivering what it forecast. On coordination, PM²-Agile adjusts type, format, granularity, language and frequency of information for non-agile audiences, and identifies three groups of reporting and planning units — delivery units, functional units and work units — which should be linked so stakeholders get a clear view of execution and delivery. RASCI p.84: BM I, PM A, TeCo R, PrOw I, ArOw I, ATeM S. Pages 29-30, 83-85.
notePlain: Rule: the Development Status Report says how the team is progressing towards the development goals, and it becomes part of the project's own reporting. It carries cost, schedule, scope, risks, issues, changes and forecasts, and it can follow each iteration and each release (page 83). Its key element is the burndown chart, at two levels. The iteration burndown chart shows remaining effort in points or hours. It is the main tool for understanding the current iteration and should be updated often, preferably daily, so the team can react by cutting scope, reducing the ambition of an item, or finding a better approach (page 84). The release burndown chart shows functionality left, not effort, and whether the team is delivering what it forecast (page 84). For coordination, PM²-Agile changes the type, format, detail, language and frequency of information for audiences that do not work in an agile way, and names three groups of reporting units: delivery units, functional units and work units. These should be linked together so stakeholders get a clear view (pages 29 and 30). Who is who: the Team Coordinator is Responsible, the Project Manager is Accountable, and the Product Owner is only Informed. Pages 29 to 30 and 83 to 85.
